title: Low-Stress Training, Trellising and SCROG Principles

content.overview: Low-stress training reshapes plant architecture by positioning shoots rather than intentionally removing large amounts of tissue. Bending, tying, trellising, and screen-based training can redistribute dominance, improve access, and manage canopy height when applied gradually.

vocabulary.definition: Canopy manipulation that bends or positions shoots without deliberately causing major tissue damage.
A support structure used to position and support branches or shoots.
Screen-of-green training in which shoots are distributed through or beneath a support screen to shape the canopy.
Relative suppression of lateral growth by a dominant shoot apex.

sections.title: Bending changes shoot position and dominance
sections.body: Repositioning the main shoot can reduce its vertical advantage and allow lateral branches to contribute more strongly to canopy development.

sections.title: Support structures create spatial control
sections.body: Trellises and screens can separate branches, maintain target height, and support reproductive weight. They also influence access for inspection, irrigation, and pruning.

sections.title: Training should respond to growth
sections.body: Plants continue changing after shoots are positioned. Repeated small adjustments are usually more controllable than forcing a mature rigid stem into a large bend at once.

sections.title: Uniform structure still requires measurement
sections.body: A visually flat canopy can still contain large light-intensity differences. Training outcomes should be checked with crop-level light and microclimate observations.

workedExamples: If one leader grows far above neighboring branches, gradual bending and support can redistribute height without removing the apex.
If a screen is overcrowded, adding more shoots may worsen shading; evaluate spacing rather than treating every empty opening as a target.

A grower fills every trellis opening early, then finds overlapping branches and shaded interior growth later. The learner recognizes that screen occupancy is a spacing problem, not a goal to maximize.

After repositioning dominant shoots, canopy height becomes more even but PPFD still varies widely. The learner verifies fixture distribution and leaf overlap instead of assuming LST solved the whole light problem.
commonMistakes: Making severe bends in rigid mature tissue.
Packing too many shoots into a screen.
Assuming a flat canopy automatically has uniform PPFD.
Overtightening ties so stems are constricted as they thicken.
Training without preserving access for scouting, irrigation and sanitation.
content.practicalApplication: Define the desired canopy footprint and height, position vigorous shoots gradually, secure them without girdling stems, maintain inspection access, and verify the resulting light distribution and airflow.
content.summary: Low-stress training uses positioning and support to shape architecture with relatively low tissue injury. Effective use depends on gradual adjustment, spacing, plant vigor, and measured canopy conditions.

blocks.title: LST changes geometry without removing the main source tissue
blocks.body: Bending and positioning alter shoot angle, height and local dominance while preserving most leaf and stem tissue. The value comes from redistributing architecture with relatively low recovery cost.

blocks.title: LST decisions should solve a measurable problem

items.title: Define the target shape
items.body: Set desired height, footprint and access.

items.title: Apply small adjustments
items.body: Reposition over time rather than in one severe bend.

items.title: Reassess growth
items.body: Plants continue changing after each adjustment.

items.title: Verify with measurements
items.body: Check PPFD, access and microclimate rather than appearance alone.

blocks.title: The screen is full, but the canopy is worse
blocks.setting: Nearly every trellis opening contains a shoot, but branches overlap and interior leaves remain shaded.
options: More filled openings always means better SCROG
Shoot density is too high for the available space
blocks.answer: Shoot density is too high for the available space.
blocks.feedback: SCROG is a spacing and distribution system, not a contest to occupy every opening.

blocks.title: Plan an LST intervention
blocks.instructions: Use a canopy diagram with four dominant shoots and several shaded laterals.
prompts: Identify any access problems created by the plan.
State what PPFD or geometry measurement will verify success.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Low-stress training works when it improves measured canopy geometry and access with minimal recovery cost.
